title: Keeping family apart from the music scene; accusations of a studio clique
summary: Matassa kept his family separate, spent long hours with musicians, and says he went out to find players rather than favor a clique.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: And we mentioned Joe. Who else in the music business in that sphere were you close to?

Let me preface all of this by saying that I made an immense effort over all my time in the music business not to become part and parcel of the music scene. I kept my kids and my wife separate from that. And I did because I felt I could deal with some of the people that I dealt with and maybe not be scarred too badly. But I didn't want them to have to. And so I kept that, my family life, really separate. There were maybe three people in the whole business that ever came to my house, you know, and that kind of thing except for Al Young who used to come regularly and fall drunk into the front door. And I'd have to, you know, take him around and get him coffee and get him sober and bring him home. But so prefacing by that, I spent an enormous amount of time with all these people. I mean, there were times when I didn't get home for two days and things like that, you know. So I spent an enormous amount of time with these people, out eating and drinking at their houses and wherever, in their apartments and this kind of stuff, you know. And I got to know an awful lot of people on a person-to-person basis. And the memories of some of that is painful, you know. I mean, it's just hard to...
Did you, in a sense, try to keep your, and sometimes keep yourself at a distance from the record company people in that the musicians, artists, people would lump you in?
Well, let me tell you what, what, what happened, some of the things that happened.
Sort of a, the co-op, the white establishment.

Well, fortunately, fortunately, there were enough black people, for instance, who, who, who lived cheek by jowl with me in, in many ways. You know, so I didn't have that problem with those people because they knew me. But there were, there were other guys, black and white, who, who, who used to complain about the, the, the studio click. Mm-hmm. They couldn't get to do sessions and they, they didn't play on record dates and they didn't get to record. And, uh, um, so, so far as I know, I try not to, to, to discriminate against somebody because they weren't in my little group or something like that. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Because, because I made it a practice to, to go out and listen. You know, I hung out. In my early days, I spent an awful lot of time in, in clubs and bars and even people's houses listening to who was playing what. Yeah. And, and, and then when somebody would come in and say, well, we need, you know, a band, I would, I would go find them. You know, they, they didn't come, they didn't have agents calling me up saying, get a gig for some, so I'd go find them at their, at their houses, where they worked, stuff like that. Excuse me. Strangling my own juice here. Uh, and, and, uh, and I took people out when, when guys came in, record companies looking for somebody to record. I took them to clubs and, and places to, and, and suggested that they go, uh, hear people and record people. I didn't always have a lot of influence with it, you know.
Well, but just that you, you were taking them places.
